utterances.text: I believe that it is within the ambit of this report to state what kind of order or orders were given by the Minister of National Defence, Bogdan Subotic on the 16th of April and then to show how the police in the RS Ministry of Internal Affairs proceeded to implement that order on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. But that -- for that very general proposition, you've basically cited Mr. Subotic's full mobilisation order there. Now, in the context of the war having begun in early April, that was not a particularly unusual move, was it?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The unusual move to mobilise?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't state what is usual or unusual, but the fact is that that is the order that he issued on that date. And as I proceed to then show, the -- his order was subsequently cited at the regional and the municipal level in further, more specific orders that were implemented by the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, I think we'll leave that paragraph, Mr. Nielsen, and we will move on to paragraph 194 of your report. Now, in the last two sentences of paragraph 194, you indicate this: "The police cited attacks on Serbs and the JNA, TO, and VRS as factors necessitating the disarmament of non-Serbs." The next sentence: "Yet these were largely small and isolated incidents that stood in stark contrast to the military and police operations undertaken against non-Serbs in the course of the disarmament drive." Now, in the context of that statement that you've made there about"largely small and isolated incidents," Mr. Nielsen, you're not in a position, are you, to put forward that opinion merely on the analysis of the internal documents of the MUP, which is the focus of your report?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That particular sentence of the report is a sentence constructed on the basis of the MUP reports filed at the municipal, regional, and national levels in 1992. It is an aggregate statement. However, it is an absolutely correct observation to state that in making that assertion, I was also informed by military documents - for example, from the 1st Krajina Corps, to which I've had access and which often mention joint police and military operations, particularly in the Autonomous Region of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. So in essence you're basing that sentence, are you, you indicate to the Trial Chamber, on the basis of your examination of documents specifically relating to ARK? Correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that particular case, yes, that is -- that is correct. It is in fact the case, as the Trial Chamber may know, that the document collections that we have at OTP with respect to the police are quantitatively biassed in favour of ARK, which is to say that the quantity of material that we have in from the RS in 1992 is to a very large extent based on the police in the Autonomous Region of Krajina. One of the things that I have tried to do as an analyst is to remedy that by collecting additional document collections from the police from other regions of the RS, such as the Sarajevo, Eastern Bosnia, and Herzegovina regions.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Nielsen, just going on to paragraph 196 of your report. You state there that "There is some evidence that some Crisis Staffs did not control the military or police." Now, again, you haven't put yourself forward as an expert on Crisis Staffs, but there is, of course, is there not, significant evidence that Crisis Staffs did not control the military or the police, as opposed to putting it in this negative fashion, there is some evidence that some Crisis Staffs did not control the military or the police.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As an aggregate observation based on my examination of hundreds of thousands of pages of RS MUP documents, in 1992 it is generally the case, especially during the first six months of the ministry's existence, that the Crisis Staffs frequently issued orders or made at the very least suggestions for work or actions to be taken by the police in municipalities as well as at the regional level. The Law on Internal Affairs from 1992, the RS Law on Internal Affairs, provided for such suggestions or orders to be made and carried out by the police at the municipal level as long as such actions demanded by the police did not contradict the Law on Internal Affairs and did not require the police to carry out actions that fell outside the purview of the Ministry of Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Nevertheless, Mr. Nielsen, you don't put yourself forward as an expert in relation to the functioning of Crisis Staffs and their connections; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I'm not sure it's necessary to continue re-asking that same question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, it is part of the rituals, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Part of the ritual, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm happy to move on from that topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think it's quite clear in what respects Mr. Nielsen presents himself as an expert.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: If I might have a moment, Your Honour. I'm just looking for a particular reference in a report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If Mr. Nielsen needs some time, you may take some time as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Nielsen, just in relation to paragraph 278 of your report, you refer there to, in the third sentence: "From Prijedor Drljaca reported that there were no detention facilities except for Manjaca." Do you see that reference there in paragraph 278?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. And there's a reference there to a document of the 28th of August, 1992. It's quite clear, is it not, that Mr. Drljaca was not in fact reporting up the line the correct situation in his municipality, was he?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular dispatch or as a matter of general practice?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: As a matter of general practice.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree. I do believe, based on the materials that I've examined from SJB Prijedor and CSB Banja Luka that Mr. Drljaca reported on a regular and, to the best of my ability to ascertain this, accurate manner to Stojan Zupljanin, his superior, at CSB Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: We'll come back to that at a later stage, Mr. Nielsen. Now, in relation to paragraph 275 of your report, you indicate that "On the 19th of August, 1992 Karadzic ordered the VRS and the MUP to treat all prisoners in accordance with international norms and to cooperate with international organisations." And you also indicate: "This order was issued a reiteration of a presidential order of the 6th of June, 1992." Now, you're aware of a number of orders coming from Mr. Karadzic in relation to the treatment of prisoners and treatment in accordance with international norms; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, I believe I cite two of them right here.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed. And, in fact, there's more than two.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, moving on to your page 293 -- sorry, page 84, paragraph 293. You deal there with problems in policing and a complaint there from Mr. Zupljanin and this question of prisoners arriving without any supporting documentation or the reason for their arrest and there's further aspects that are covered there. It's quite clear, is it not - and as one might expect in wartime - that there was quite a state of chaos in relation to what was occurring there? The matters that Mr. Zupljanin refers to.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not agree that this is a state of chaos. What I do know, based on the documents, is that there were mutual recriminations between the VRS and the RS MUP in the late summer of 1992, July and August in particular, in which both sides, the military and the police, accused each other of rounding up large numbers of persons in the Autonomous Region of Krajina and then -- I believe the word used in the documents themselves is "dumping" those persons in detention facilities that would have to be controlled and guarded and operated, et cetera, by the other side. So, for example, RS MUP complains that the VRS and earlier the TOs have rounded up thousands of people in Bosanski Novi and neighbouring municipalities, like Sanski Most, and have not compiled any dossiers or other records as to why these people have been detained and then have given these detention facilities for MUP to operate. That is something that we see, for example, at the 11 July meeting in Belgrade as a big point of discontent among the police officers. On the other hand, here we see the reverse process. In August, when Simo Drljaca starts to shut down Omarska, Trnopolje, and Keraterm and transfer a large number of prisoners to Manjaca, which is a VRS-controlled facility, the VRS complain that the persons being transferred to Manjaca are arriving without any form of supporting documentation. I would not describe that situation as chaos because during the very same period, as I note in my report, in particular in the section on detention facilities and also in the section on the National Security Service, the police demonstrated a capability to keep very accurate numerical records on the number of detainees in those facilities and the number of interrogations carried out of those detainees. And indeed they also kept detailed records of the number of criminal complaints resulting from these interrogations.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Nielsen, I note that you disagree with my description of "chaos" or "chaotic," but you would agree, in light of what you've indicated, that there certainly appeared to be a lack of coordination; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this particular juncture, what we see in the police documents - I cannot speak about the contents -- or I cannot speak authoritatively on the contents of the military documents - is a rather rapid rush, driven by external events, and in particular international attention on the detention facilities in the Autonomous Region of Krajina, to shut down these facilities or at a minimum greatly reduce the number of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. persons detained in such facilities. In fact, we see in at least one or two documents during this period explicit references in ARK by police chiefs of municipalities to the desire not to be embarrassed internationally by these detention facilities. So they seem in a great rush to hand these persons over either to Manjaca or to shut down the facilities and get those persons out of those facilities as rapidly as possible. That, it appears, based on the VRS's complaints, led to a certain amount of disorder, but I do not agree with an assertion that this is a situation of chaos.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. So you'd rather use the term "disorder" than chaos; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think, if I may use your word, a "lack of coordination" is an acceptable interpretation, and indeed we note throughout the summer of 1992 that the VRS and the MUP had rather heated discussions on a number of topic, such as, for example, since you referred to paragraph 290, the massacre of Muslims at Koricanske Stijene.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Mr. Nielsen, moving on to another aspect of your report, and that is in relation to paragraph 337 and following, and that is where you're dealing with the 1992 RS MUP draft draft annual report. Now, of course, as an analyst, you would agree with me that it's important in terms of analysing this sort of document to take into account that often what is true must be distinguished from what is self-serving by the writers and also what is propaganda; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, without engaging in any epistemological debate, yes, I would say that, generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And just in relation to paragraph 347, where you indicate that "The president and the members of the Presidency had received more than 80 documents in the course of the past eight months," of course you've never seen any list produced by the Ministry of what exactly those reports are; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have already stated, I have never seen any exhaustive list of either the 80 documents listed in that sentence or the 90 documents listed in the earlier sentence. What can be said by process of logical deduction is that the 17 July report that we saw last week in which the MUP had produced a report that was in handwriting destined for the president of the Presidency and the president of the government would certainly have been one of those documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Nielsen, I note that as part of your CV you have spoken on the topic of Western historians and the problem of objectivity in historical research, and of course this issue is one that one takes into consideration when -- when dealing with history and also in relation to writing reports of the nature that you've written; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have my CV in front of me. I believe you're referring to an article, rather than a speech. But, yes, I am, as a professional historian, well aware of the debates and follow the debates on epistemology and objectivity in historical research.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And part of what you -- or it's in fact an abstract of your lecture rather than an article. It says "Western historians and the problem of objectivity in historical research."

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for reminding me. That was a -- actually a talk I gave in Belgrade at the -- at a higher education centre in Belgrade and then subsequently developed for an article that was published in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And in relation to that article, that lecture, the -- the goal of the lecture, of course, was to open a debate about the subjectivity of research in Serbian and former Yugoslav historiography; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was introduce an audience both in Serbia and in Croatia to a very vigorous debate about historical positivism and epistemology that had been started in the 1980s and 1970s in North America and Western Europe.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, of course, as we all know, every researcher has a subjective frame of reference, and the question must always be asked: How is it possible to write history or a report of the nature that you're writing objectively? What do you consider to be the factors that must be taken into account to ensure that what you write is as objective as possible?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the first and most important factor is that once the ambit of a particular historical inquiry is set, that one tries to read as widely and extensively as possible on the material -- or on the given subject. In particular, as a historian, I differentiate between primary and secondary sources. That is why I rely to a very extensive extent in this report, as I did also in my dissertation and earlier work that I've done, on primary sources; that is to say, sources produced contemporaneously by the actors involved in the subject at hand.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. No further questions on -- or no, well, before I leave that topic, what else do you need, in your opinion? It's not just that aspect, is it?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, certainly what one is taught and what one practices as a critical historian is critical comparison of documents produced by various sides and in various languages. That is one of the reasons why in the leadership research team everyone who has produced expert reports has read the documents in the original source language, as there are often, as we have seen during this testimony, discrepancies and particular terminology that can be better understood if one speaks the language. I also think that, as a general point, it is of course the case that one has to remain open to documents that are showing evidence or information that is not consistent with a hypothesis formulated at the outset of inquiry. That's a standard axiom of proper historical research.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Nielsen.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if that's an appropriate juncture to take a break. I have to go and get some documents at this point because I've proceeded rather more quickly than I had anticipated at this point.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS

utterances.text: Now, Mr. Nielsen, I think you have a copy of the English and the B/C/S before you?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]

utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And of course we can have -- we can form ourselves an opinion on whether this is legible or not legible at all or that it might be difficult to read it, but usually one reads in the context of the language one understands.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. I'm happy to leave that topic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS

utterances.text: Now, Mr. Nielsen, I just want to take you to footnotes 352 and 353 of your report. And here, Mr. Nielsen, I have copies of the footnoted material for 353 and 352 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Although, at a certain moment we'd like, of course, to have the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there's more to distribute, Ms. Loukas, then please give it already to Madam Usher so that we'll be --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: In any event, you'll recall that earlier today I was asking you some questions about Simo Drljaca.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Excellent. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER

So I -- I didn't intend to -- to inadvertently mislead the Court into thinking it was footnote 354.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I think we're dealing with too many footnotes, quite frankly, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We try to reduce them, as you know, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for the first page, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Nielsen, we are dealing with the document entitled "Report, reception centre in the territory of the Prijedor municipality."

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have that document in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And that is referenced in which footnote, so that we can ensure that the transcript is accurate?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I referenced that in footnote 354 and in footnote 355, and I may also -- and I reference it in footnote 358, and I may also reference it in other footnotes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, just in relation to questions I was asking you previously in relation to Mr. Drljaca. You'll note there -- and I think it's -- it's on page 5 of the English version and I think page 5 of the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, what English version?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Oh, I'm dealing with the version I have in front of me. I just referenced that to ensure that we had the proper reference for the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I only received a copy, I think, of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So did we. You said there were no --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That's the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But if it's -- if it's footnote -- if it's tab 34, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, once again, Your Honour, this is footnote 354. That's not the tab to which I was referring.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: 352 and 353 is that tab.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's proceed and see how far we come.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, where were we, Mr. Nielsen? In any event, you'll recall that I was asking you some questions in relation to Mr. Drljaca? You recall those questions earlier today, Mr. Nielsen?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yeah. And in relation to the document before you, do you have the portion that indicates "Facilities in Omarska are supplied with water. They have the necessary number of sanitary facilities and the bathrooms, dining hall, and the halls in which the prisoners slept over. They also had sufficient number of the working areas where the processing took place"? Do you see that portion on the --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do see that portion.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And -- and further it describes other aspects: "The primary medical service is secured for the prisoners. The food was prepared in the RZR and was distributed in the restaurant organised on the principle of self-service to prisoners, official staff, and part of the RZR staff who remained working there to maintain the premises." Do you see the portion that I'm referring to there?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, just in relation to that, Mr. Nielsen, it's quite clear, is it not, that there's the distinct possibility that Mr. Drljaca is not sharing accurate information; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't want to speculate; however, I would note that the conditions that he observes -- or that he believes obtain at that point in Omarska, and for that matter in Trnopolje and the other detention facilities that he discusses in this report, are in contrast to the kinds of conditions that were observed for these types of facilities at the 11 July meeting in Belgrade, whereas Zupljanin was present and discussed this matter with the minister, among others.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Nevertheless --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Nielsen, I think, as a matter of fact, that that was not the question. Perhaps it would assist you to know that in the adjudicated facts there appears a quite different picture from these circumstances. And I think what Ms. Loukas is trying to find out is where you earlier said that Mr. Drljaca was a, well, reliable reporter, if that's at least the issue, Ms. Loukas, how you could reconcile that part of your testimony with this part of this report, where it appears that it might well have been not such an accurate description of Omarska.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, to answer the question, I certainly am familiar with events at Omarska from a variety of sources, and in this report I am trying to include only any information that I have based on the documents of RS MUP themselves. With respect to the specific question at hand, I would state that this report, along with a series of reports that I cite in this specific section, most particularly the report produced jointly by the Ministry of Justice and the Ministry of Internal Affairs at the time, presented, I think, one could safely say, a very rosy picture of the conditions obtaining in those detention facilities at the time. Now, I'm not in a position to state how Mr. Zupljanin or anyone else in the ministry reconciled that picture that Drljaca is giving in this report with earlier contrary information that they had clearly received because they discussed that at the 11 July meeting in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the issue is how you reconcile your earlier part of your testimony whereupon a question by Ms. Loukas - I don't remember the exact words - but was Mr. Drljaca usually reliably reporting it or something like that. I could find it. But you confirmed that. And now Ms. Loukas confronts you with a report where you said, "Well, from what I know, it's a very rosy report," where you seemed not to have included that in your previous answer when asked about the reliability of Mr. Drljaca's reporting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I maintain my position that Mr. Drljaca reported on a regular basis throughout the summer of 1992. As to the reliability of his reporting, certainly there are occasions, the Koricanske Stijene episode is one of them, when Zupljanin, among other, was not content with what Drljaca was reporting back up to Mr. Zupljanin. However, I would note that there is no indication in the documents that I've examined pursuant to this report that Zupljanin complained about the contents of this report. In fact, this report is, as it says at the outset, produced following a decision by CSB Banja Luka and it was collated into larger reports for the detention facilities in ARK as a whole that were then handed to the minister and were also passed on to other government ministries. I do not see any indication that Mr. Zupljanin subsequently complained about the unreliability of Mr. Drljaca's reporting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just, then -- you were asked: "It's quite clear, is it not, that Mr. Drljaca was not in fact reporting up the line the correct situation in his municipality, was he?" And you said: "In this particular dispatch or as a matter of general practice?" Then Ms. Loukas said: "As a matter of general practice." And then you said: "I disagree. I do believe, based on the materials that I've examined from SJB Prijedor and CSB Banja Luka, that Mr. Drljaca reported on a regular and to the best of my ability to ascertain this accurate manner to Stojan Zupljanin, his superior at CSB Banja Luka." Ms. Loukas is now confronting you with at least this report, which seems, also in your own view, not to be an accurate account of ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand Your Honour's point, and I would definitely state that I cannot explain the -- the discrepancy as -- as Your Honour has explained it right here. What I can state is that I am aware not from Mr. Drljaca but from other subordinates of Stojan Zupljanin during this period that there was a great amount of concern - this is voiced both in Sanski Most by the head of the SJB there, and in Kljuc by the head of the SJB there - that this particular phase of intense international scrutiny of the RS was not the appropriate moment to report on any detrimental issues, in particular any potential information regarding abuses of non-Serbs in the ARK region.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Loukas, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I took it that this was the point. You would like to directly confront the witness -- the expert with this matter. I took I want that was the point.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would choose a microphone, any of the three, and use one of them at least.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. I just need to go over to where I have some transcript on the laptop.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Nielsen, you'll recall that just prior to the break I was asking you some questions about subjective frames of reference and writing of history and reports. That's page -- bottom of page 53, beginning of page 54.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall that.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And just prior to the break, you indicated: "I also think that as a general point it is of course the case that one has to remain open to documents that are showing evidence or information that is not consistent with a hypothesis formulated at the outset of inquiry. That's a standard axiom of proper historical research." Mr. Nielsen, in your subjective opinion, have you adhered to that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. standard?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Loukas. Mr. Krajisnik, if you would have any additional questions for Mr. Nielsen, you may put them to him now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since I'm looking at the time and I do know that we must allow some time for the Judges' questions and possible additional questions, I'm going to try and keep my question as brief as possible. I would like to ask Dr. Nielsen to tell us whether he knows about how many attempts at peace plans there had been in Bosnia and Herzegovina prior to the Dayton Agreement.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not, as I have stated, an expert on international peace plans in Bosnia and Herzegovina either before, during, or after the conflict; however, I am aware that there were numerous such attempts at peace plans.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I would furthermore ask you to tell us whether in any one of those peace plans there had been provisions for the police force to be a single force at the Bosnia-Herzegovina level. Let me clarify this: Do you agree that in all those plans the police force would be at the entity level, in this case in the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know that the police figure prominently in all of these discussions and that in many of the plans the police forces were to be at the entity, cantonal or other sub-national level. I also know, however, that with the exception of the Dayton Accords, that particular aspect of police structuring in Bosnia and Herzegovina was never accepted by the Muslims in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Doctor, I asked you whether in all plans there were provisions for the police force to be within the area of competence of entities and that none of the parties objected to that provision.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I am not familiar with the details of all of these plans, of which I believe there are many; however, I do know that the, as I stated, the Muslims were not willing on several occasions to accept for the police to be steered at an entity level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I would like to state that in no peace plan or talks for that peace plan the Muslim side never complained about this particular provision. And let me just remind this gathering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I take it that you object to the question as it was started by Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, the question on whether -- the witness two times said that: "The particular aspect of police structuring in Bosnia and Herzegovina at the entity level was never accepted by the Muslims." He said that two times. You are not allowed to now tell the witness that it was different. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: As to Cutilheiro's plan, was police supposed to be within the area of competence of the entities and did all parties accept that clause?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge - and again, I am not an expert on the Cutilheiro Plan - it was in fact not a plan per se but there were several agreements that were reached tentatively under the auspices of Mr. Cutilheiro's directorship. I do know that Momcilo Mandic and Stojan Zupljanin, as I explained earlier today, did make reference to implementation of the Sarajevo agreement at the outset of April 1992; however, the other side, specifically the Muslim side in SRBiH MUP, did not at any point agree that such an agreement had been reached or should be implemented through the establishment of separate ethnic Ministries of Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I don't think that that is an answer to my question, but I can move on to another question now. I would like to ask you, since we don't have much time available, to simply say whether you do or do not know something about this: Do you know that in all plans there were provisions for the division of Sarajevo? What I mean are the peace plans which were being put forward by the international community and they were being put to all three parties. Just say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer the question because I'm not familiar with those plans.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: So you do not know.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I cannot answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I would just like to remind you: You said that on the 28th of February, Constitution -- the Constitution of the Republika Srpska was approved. You probably meant the 27th of March, 1992.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would certainly defer on all points of dating, except -- I may have been confusing the Law on Internal Affairs, which was adopted on the 28th of February, with the date on the Constitution. Again, on such points of general political developments, I would defer to Mr. Treanor's report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Are you familiar with Lord Owen's book "The Balkan Odyssey"?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am. I've read the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Do you know that on page 88 he quoted some attitudes of the international community and what the international community had in mind as a solution for Bosnia and Herzegovina? I'm just going to quote this now. There were five proposals: "The international community suggested either a centralised state or a centralised federal state within which significant functions would be held by four to ten regions, a loose federation of three ethnic units without geographical continuity, a loose confederation of three ethnically clear republics with a considerable degree of independence and perhaps even in such fields as security, and the fifth proposal, a Muslim state with the proviso that the Serbs would -- the Serb part would belong to the former Yugoslavia and the Croat part would go with Croatia." You've probably read this in the book.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that Mr. Izetbegovic and I, myself, I signed on behalf of the Serb side. Do you know that they signed a declaration --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... it's just that on the transcript I think Mr. Nielsen's answer does not appear. It's just got "previous translation continues."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, again, if you speak closer to the microphone, we can hear what you say.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed. Your Honours will notice that on the transcript the answer by Mr. Nielsen was not recorded before Mr. Krajisnik proceeded to his next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. When you said -- when you were asked: "you've probably read this in book," what was your answer, Mr. Nielsen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have read that answer in the book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then we --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The reason is that Mr. Nielsen replied before the interpretation was finished and so they were both speaking at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not blaming either the transcribers nor the interpreters for it, but just to have it clear on the record. Mr. Nielsen, you're invited not to answer the question before the interpretation is ended because I do understand that you understand Mr. Krajisnik in his own language. But nevertheless wait until translation is finished. Please proceed, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: In the course of your testimony, you declared that on the 15th of May, 1992 the national security committee reached a decision about immediate threat. You might have made a mistake. The decision was made by two members of the Presidency. Do you agree with me that you might have made a mistake there?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First of all, Your Honour, it would be helpful if we could have some reference to the portion of the transcript where that response is assertedly contained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Loukas, could you help him? Otherwise, I'll try to find it on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. We'll make endeavours in that regard, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps it would be simpler to ask the witness who took the decision.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In this particular case, I would, again, defer to Mr. Treanor's report, which I believe provides an answer to that question. It is not a point that I have examined in detail in my report.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have the record here and the decision. If necessary, we could put it on the ELMO. I would make the suggestion to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is that in evidence in one way or the other yet or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I believe it is, Your Honour, and I believe it was a subject of Mr. Treanor's testimony. However, I think the question has been answered. Mr. Krajisnik asked: "Do you agree with me that you might have made a mistake there?" And Mr. Nielsen said, "I would refer to Mr. Treanor on that particular point."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you'd say whatever Mr. Treanor said about it is -- should be the correct answer, and you did not deal with it personally. Perhaps just for -- to make it very practical, could -- could we have the report on the ELMO for one second so that we can all convince ourselves on -- on who seems to be the author of the decision. Madam Usher, could you ... And then we'll try to find out -- perhaps, Ms. Loukas, you could assist Mr. Krajisnik to find out whether this is in evidence, yes or not, the document. But I took it on your authority, Mr. Tieger, that it is. Looking at the document, Mr. Nielsen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I see at the top of the page that's currently on the ELMO, point 3 up there states: "Decisions and conclusion -- or decision and conclusions." It's a little bit vague. But it's -- then goes on to state: "Regarding or with respect to the security situation in the Serbian Republic in Bosnia and Herzegovina, it is evaluated that the conditions have arisen that the Presidency of the republic should be suggested to proclaim a situation of imminent danger of war."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Any further questions in this respect, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. And could we please place the decision on the ELMO. The decision was published in the Official Gazette and it's attached to this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I see the decision. I'm going to have to remove it from the ELMO very briefly; otherwise, I can't read it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The decision that I see here is -- states that "On the basis of Article 81 of the Constitution of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and on the suggestion of the government, the Presidency of the Serb Republic Bosnia and Herzegovina makes a decision regarding the proclamation of a state of imminent threat -- imminent danger of war." And then the following and final point states that "Mobilisation of the TO for the entire territory of Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina is ordered." It is signed by Plavsic and Koljevic and dated the 15th of April, 1992. And I do believe - although it is possible that I misspoke - that when I very briefly dealt with this issue, that I said 15 of April and not 15 of May, as was earlier suggested.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Is that decision -- is that decision based on the document that you were reading a minute ago?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the document I was reading a minute ago - I'll just put the first page of it out on the ELMO - is a set of minutes from the joint meeting of the Security Council and the government of the RS on the 15th of April, 1992. And the decision in the gazette to which Mr. Krajisnik refers not to the Security Council; it actually only refers to the government. But I believe the two to be connected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So I do understand that actually you -- you referred earlier to the 15th of April as the date on which the threat of war -- a threat of war was declared by the National Security Council; whereas, Mr. Krajisnik has now drawn our attention to a publication of a decision which is attributed to another organ and is published, as we just saw it on the ELMO. Ms. Loukas, would you please be so kind to verify whether both the documents are in evidence at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: As I understand it, both the documents are in evidence with the evidence of Mr. Treanor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And I stand to be corrected by Mr. Tieger if that's not correct, but that's my understanding of the relevant documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know if both documents are at the same tab, but we would be looking at P64A, P65 binder 11, tab 120.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So there seems to be an initial agreement that this is in evidence and the witness has now given the answers. Mr. Krajisnik, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I just have one more question to put to the witness. The letter that was sent by Mr. Mandic, are you aware of the fact that it was sent when the Brussels conference was being held. The entire delegation was in Brussels at the time. Are you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not -- I was not aware of that fact, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: And in relation to that question, did Mr. Mandic have the right to send such a letter and was this right based on a law of any kind?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the dispatch dated 31 of March, 1992, Momcilo Mandic finds a legal foundation in sending that dispatch and in asking people to implement it in the laws that have been brought in the Assembly of the Serbian People in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Certainly as an assistant minister he had the power to send dispatches to everybody in the ministry on a variety of questions; however, on this specific point, I would refer to the -- the Court to the dispatch of the same day by Delimustafic in which he, as Momcilo Mandic's boss, notes that there is -- that this act was done without consultation with the rest of the ministry and that he orders the persons who have received the dispatch not to proceed to implement it. Therefore, there is, as far as I can tell, no legal basis within SRBiH MUP regulations and laws to send a dispatch to form a separate Ministry of Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to thank the Trial Chamber and the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, any need to put further questions to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Judge Hanoteau as a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I simply wanted to understand a certain issue. In your report, I can see in one of the footnotes, page 79, CBS Banja Luka report, page 83 - and I'm picking these footnotes at random - footnote 119, dispatch of SJB -- from the SJB Prijedor; 425, dispatch from the Kljuc SJB. Who were they addressed to? Were these reports or dispatches always sent to the same bodies or people? I just want to clarify this to make it easier for us to read your report. How should these footnotes be interpreted and should one draw the conclusion that these reports, these letters, were always addressed to the ministry or on each occasions is it necessary to consult the report in question, the document in order to know who the given document was in fact addressed to?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the case of the dispatches that originate at the SJB level, unless I have noted otherwise, the recipient of the dispatch is the CSB to which that SJB answers. So in the case of Kljuc and Prijedor that Your Honour mentioned, those SJBs throughout 1992 report to CSB Banja Luka, and unless otherwise noted, a dispatch from those SJBs would be destined to Mr. Zupljanin in Banja Luka. I was at the time that I wrote this report and also at the time that I revised this report under the impression that all documents that are cited in this report would be made available in B/C/S and in English to the Chamber. I am aware that that has changed a bit, and I, as a consequence, do apologise if there is any questions that are left open about the destination of these dispatches. If it is something that is of interest to the Chamber or to any of the parties, I am at your disposal in creating a full list of the destinatories [sic] of these dispatches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And a second subject that has nothing to do with what I've already asked you about: You have spoken at length about the MUP, the police force that you have called the MUP. In the course of this trial, we have often heard the SUP being mentioned. Would it be possible for you today to tell us what the difference between the SUP and MUP is? Perhaps you are not an expert in the matter, but you might be able to clarify this for me.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed I can, Your Honour. The SUP prior to 1990 referred to both the Municipal Secretariat for Internal Affairs, which in B/C/S is "Sekretarijat Unutrasnjih Poslova," as well as to the Republican Secretariat of Internal Affairs, abbreviated R-S-U-P, or RSUP. Once the 1990 SRBiH Law on Internal Affairs was passed, the municipal organ for internal affairs became known as the public security station, or SJB, in full "Stanica Javne Bezbjednosti" in B/C/S. To this day in Bosnia-Herzegovina, it is the case that the wider population will colloquially refer to the SJB as the SUP. The reason for that, I believe, is very simple: It is much easier to say "SUP" than S-U-B, which would be the abbreviation in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Judge Hanoteau, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What sort of activities were they involved in? Could you be precise?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The SUP prior to 1990 had much more extensive -- a much more extensive ambit in interacting with municipal organs of -- such as the Municipal Assembly than the SJB did later on. And indeed, if I may refer the Court to the planning documents that we discussed at the very outset of my testimony in tabs, I believe it was, either 2 and 3 or 3 and 4 from October and September 1991. The Bosnian Serbs looked back with considerable nostalgia to the pre-1990 period exactly for that reason, because the Municipal Assemblies prior to 1990 had been in the position to interact much more freely with the police instead of having to seek constant approval from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Tieger. Would you like to help me?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Perhaps, Your Honour. I hope so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As I understood His Honour's question, he was asking about the difference or distinction between the MUP and the SUP. Is it the case that the MUP is the whole thing and the SUP is part of that thing at the municipal level? In a -- in a very crude nutshell.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Prior to 1990, the SUP at the municipal level is part of the RSUP at the republican level, which is in turn part of the SSUP, the Federal Secretariat for Internal Affairs at the federal level. After 1990 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. I apologise for interfering, but before 1990, could you tell me what the role of this institution was. What sort of activities was it involved in? What was the purpose of this body?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is Your Honour referring to the Republican Secretariat or the SUP at the municipal level?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let's start with the republican level and then let's deal with the municipal level. I'm interested in both, because I would like to understand the structure that existed. I would like to know what we are in fact discussing.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we start at the republican level, the Republican Secretariat for Internal Affairs had essentially the function of organising the broad area of functions, including policing, known as internal affairs in Bosnia-Herzegovina and coordinating those actions throughout the republic. It was subordinate to the Federal Secretariat, which was located in Belgrade, as were all of the other Republican Secretariats in the other Yugoslav republics at that time. However, per the 1974 Constitution, which gave significantly additional autonomy to the republics within Yugoslavia, there were a great deal of day-to-day policing activities and managing of public law and order in Bosnia and Herzegovina that could be done by the Ministry -- by, excuse me, the Secretariat of Internal Affairs at the republican level in coordination with the republican Presidency. At the municipal level, the SUP at the municipal level would receive its instructions and staffing directions from the centre; however, again, until 1990, there was a quite wide avenue for input from the Municipal Assemblies, in particular the Executive Councils of those Municipal Assemblies, with regard to nominations of chief of police, nomination for commander of police at the municipal level. And as I've indicated, the Municipal Assemblies could and did in practice ask the Secretariat of Internal Affairs at the municipal level to carry out tasks that would involve the use of the police at the municipal level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was before 1990. And how did this work after 1990?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: After 1990 and until the war, the Secretariat for Internal Affairs at the municipal level was replaced by the public security station. According to the 1990 Law on Internal Affairs, the municipal organs of internal affairs retained the possibility to coordinate on certain questions with the Republican Secretariat for Internal Affairs, which was now renamed the Republican Ministry for Internal Affairs. However, any such action had to take place more explicitly with permission from Sarajevo. In addition, other questions, such as staffing of the ministry, took place with a more centralised direction from Sarajevo. That is or was the main difference. There was also a funding difference because prior to 1990 the Municipal Assemblies had to a significant extent financed the police at the municipal level. And as was indicated in one of the documents on decentralising internal affairs, the police absorbed such a huge percentage of the budget in Bosnia and Herzegovina that the municipalities simply could not bear this financial burden.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Were MUPs in existence before 1990?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were called SUPs prior to 1990. 1990. Secretariats. And the title of minister systematically replaced the title of secretary in the 1990 and 1992 laws; although, Serbia proper retained the term secretariat for quite some time thereafter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just one question for you just to see whether I understood it. Do I understand that at the republican level what used to be the SUP became the MUP?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that at the municipal level what was -- used to be called the SUP, which now officially was renamed to the SJB, still was called SUP by everyone because they were used to it?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, and that colloquial usage persists to this day in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now that's -- it seems that, if I understood ... Have the questions by the Bench raised any -- they are more of an informative character, I would say, than anything else.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No questions were raised on the part of the Defence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Nielsen, this concludes your evidence. We'd like to thank you very much for coming and answering questions of the parties, of the accused, and of the Bench. You are excused.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have no time at this moment to deal any further with any exhibits, apart from some questions still to be there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, in -- on the 17th of May, we gave some guidelines as to exhibits. Part of it was that the Prosecution was invited to tender documents referred to in the expert report which are necessary to achieve the purpose of point 2. And point 2 was that the Prosecution should limit its examination to matters of central importance to the case which are likely to be controversial and which require further explanation, clarification, or illustration in terms of how the opinion was arrived at by the expert. We are now confronted with the situation where, as far as I understand, not all the documents in the three binders have been used. Point 5 of our guidance was that all remaining documentation underlying the expert report will not be admitted into evidence unless one of the parties shows good cause in light of the above or the Chamber itself specifically requests so. This seems to go in the direction that those portions of the binders that have been dealt with during the examination of the witness are suitable for admission into evidence and for any of the others, that we would need a further explanation on why we could not do without them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, thank you for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not necessarily to be done at this moment, looking at the clock as well. But I just wanted to establish what the situation was. And if we could hear from you at -- at the earliest opportunity from now on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'll be pleased to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then are there any other issues to be raised urgently at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Not on the part of the Defence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll adjourn until next Thursday, and courtroom, Madam Registrar, would be Courtroom III again. And I'd like to thank, again, the interpreters and the technicians for their assistance, going well beyond a quarter to 2.00. Thank you very much.
